title: Newsom signs four California AI workplace bills restricting ADS and surveillance
subtitle: SB 947 bars sole-ADS employment decisions from July 2027, SB 951 adds AI mass-layoff notices, and AB 1883 bans emotion-prediction and neural-data collection on employees.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: On September 30, California Governor Gavin Newsom signed a package of four AI workplace bills: SB 947, SB 951, AB 1883, and AB 1331. The highest-impact piece is SB 947 — effective July 1, 2027, it prohibits employers from relying solely on an Automated Decision System when making employment-related decisions, and requires a human reviewer to conduct an independent investigation and compile corroborating information for any disciplinary or termination decision. SB 951 amends Cal/WARN to require layoff notices to flag mass terminations caused in whole or substantial part by an AI system or other automated technology that replaces or automates positions.

AB 1883 bans AI-powered workplace surveillance tools that predict employees' emotional states or collect neural data. AB 1331 prohibits workplace surveillance tools from monitoring employees in bathrooms. The two surveillance bills, taken together, mark the first US state-level restriction on neural-data employment collection — a category that effectively did not exist in employment law 18 months ago. They also preempt a growing emotion-AI vendor segment that had marketed 'burnout detection' and 'engagement scoring' tools to HR departments.

The bills sit on top of California's existing Automated Decision Systems Regulations, which took effect October 1, 2025 and already require FEHA-covered employers to run bias testing, keep records, and offer transparency about AI used in employment decisions. The practical consequence is that California employers now face a compliance stack — ADS regulations today, SB 947 human-review mandates in July 2027, and WARN AI notices immediately — that will almost certainly become the national template as other states copy pieces of it. Colorado's AI Act, in its replaced-and-effective June 30, 2026 form, is the closest existing parallel.

A takeaway for learners: AI regulation is often described at the frontier-model level — compute thresholds, red-teaming requirements — but the regulation that actually touches most people's lives is going to look like SB 947. If you build or deploy ADS for hiring, performance, scheduling, or discipline, the practical question is no longer 'is this allowed?' but 'what documentation, human-review process, and notice workflow do I need to make it allowed?' Study the California bills early — the compliance architecture they require is portable.
